questions.q: What does sharing inheritance do for a CRM Analytics dataset?
options: It deletes rows users can't see in the source
It converts dashboards into Salesforce reports
It applies a Salesforce object's sharing logic to the dataset's rows
questions.explain: Sharing inheritance lets a dataset reuse the sharing logic of a Salesforce object so users see rows they could see in the CRM.

questions.q: Per Salesforce guidance described in this lesson, why should you also set a security predicate when using sharing inheritance?
options: Predicates decide row visibility when inheritance can't be honored, acting as a fallback
It removes the need for testing
questions.explain: When sharing settings can't be applied, for example beyond documented limits, the predicate determines what rows are visible.

questions.q: A dataset is built from several Salesforce objects. How many objects can it inherit sharing from?
questions.explain: A dataset inherits from a single object regardless of how many were used to build it; verify current limits in the docs.

questions.q: Which scenario most clearly calls for a custom security predicate?
options: Rows come from a warehouse table with a territory column
A dataset is a plain view of a single Opportunity object
questions.explain: External data has no Salesforce sharing to inherit, so a predicate on a mapping column is needed.

questions.q: What is the main ongoing cost of custom predicates compared with sharing inheritance?
options: They must be maintained manually when business rules like territories change
They require a separate Salesforce org
questions.explain: Nothing in Salesforce will update a hand-written predicate, so it needs documentation and maintenance.
